Map auth-service's dependency graph and catalog everything that changed around the incident: all deployments and config changes on 2026-04-22 (and the preceding 24-48h) across auth-service AND its upstream/downstream dependencies and shared components; identify what auth-service depends on (user DB, session/token store, cache, secrets, external IdP) and any dependencies shared with other services. Also search historical incidents for the prior bcrypt regression and similar login-latency incidents for precedent (what the fix/cause was).

Correlate onset with candidate causes: given the change events and dependency list returned by the dependency task, check metrics/logs to determine which candidate best explains the onset time - i.e., verify whether latency started exactly at a specific deployment/config change on a dependency, whether auth-service's own CPU spiked (bcrypt-style), whether a dependency's latency/error rate rose first, or whether a shared component or network/DNS degradation affected multiple services simultaneously.

events.statement: auth-service p99 latency rose from a ~89-90 ms baseline (05:30-06:42) to 2532 ms in the 06:51 bucket and held ~3.78-3.88 s through 08:57, so onset is between 06:42 and 06:51.
auth-service error_rate was 0.18-0.25% through 06:42, then spiked to 7.88% in the 06:51 bucket (max 14.76) and settled at ~14% (max 15.67) from 07:00 onward.

First 503 on /v1/auth/login is logged at 06:55:42 as 'accept queue full, returning 503 (POST /v1/auth/login)'; the immediately preceding WARN at 06:54:53 is 'worker pool saturated (active=64/64, queue=39035)'. Top ERROR pattern (372 occurrences) is the accept-queue-full 503.

auth-service CPU jumped from ~38% (05:30-06:42) to 89.96% avg (max 97.33) in the 06:51 bucket and stayed ~96-97% through 08:57 — a sharp, sustained CPU saturation coincident with the latency/error onset.
auth-service memory stayed flat at ~51-53% for the entire window and restarts were 0 throughout, so the failure is not a memory-driven crash or pod restart.

Rate-limiting on auth-service rose from ~2 req/min baseline to 487 in the 06:51 bucket and ~900 req/min (max 979.25) from 07:00 on, alongside an autoscaler message 'desired replicas 14 exceeds maxReplicas 8; cannot scale further' — indicating demand/connection pressure the service could not scale out of.

No bcrypt/CPU-regression or panic log signature appears in the auth-service WARN/ERROR set; the observed log patterns are queue/pool saturation (worker pool saturated active=64/64), accept queue full 503s, one /internal/metrics slow-request, and an NTP clock-drift message — the evidence points to saturation, not an explicit bcrypt message.

redis-cache is a SHARED datastore (shared:true) consumed by four services: auth-service, portfolio-service, pricing-engine, market-data-service — so a change or degradation in redis-cache or in any neighbouring consumer can affect auth-service login.

There was NO auth-service deployment between 2026-04-15T00:00Z and 2026-04-22T09:00Z: the deployment list for that whole week contains exactly one entry, portfolio-service v4.4.0 at 2026-04-22T05:50:00Z (status live, rolled_back_at null). The only config change in the 2026-04-15..2026-04-22 window is cfg-2801 on auth-service: log.level INFO->WARN at 2026-04-22T03:40:00Z by config-bot ("Reduce log volume"). Nothing else changed in config across all services.

Precedent HIST-101 (2025-08-14) is the prior bcrypt regression and the basis for the report's guess: symptoms 'login p99 4s, 503 on login, high cpu', root cause 'bcrypt cost factor raised 10->14 in release v6.4.0', resolution 'Rolled back v6.4.0'. Its prerequisite is an auth-service release, which is absent in the current window (finding above).

Relevant precedents for auth-service slowness that do NOT involve an auth-service release: HIST-107 (2025-12-09) 'Cold cache storm after redis failover' on redis-cache/market-data-service, root cause 'Redis primary failure promoted an empty replica', resolution 'Warmed cache; fixed replica sync checks'; and HIST-110 (2026-01-15) latency from datastore IOPS throttling. events.answer: auth-service has a small dependency set (user-db, redis-cache, kyc-provider external, and api-gateway as caller), and redis-cache is a SHARED datastore used by three other services besides auth-service. Contrary to the "bcrypt regression after an auth-service release" hypothesis, there was NO auth-service deployment in the 2026-04-15..04-22 window: the only deployment during that week (and within the incident window) is portfolio-service dep-5803 v4.4.0 at 2026-04-22T05:50:00Z — and portfolio-service is one of the four consumers of the shared redis-cache. events.summary: The saturation chain is well verified (CPU 38%->97%, worker pool 64/64 queue 39035, accept-queue-full 503s, p99 90ms->3.8s, error ~14%), and the dependency-first candidates (redis-cache + 3 co-consumers, portfolio-service) are genuinely contradicted by flat metrics across onset. H3's rejection is sound (F10/F11 falsify its prerequisite). However the two leading hypotheses H1 (in-process CPU/compute cost, 0.34) and H2 (capacity ceiling, 0.30) are separated only by the request_rate timeline versus the CPU inflection, which was never pulled — F6's rate-limited counter is a lagging proxy and all series are 9-min buckets, so temporal precedence of demand vs compute is unestablished. Both H1's confidence and its bad_deployment framing also lack any supporting change (F10/F11), and H4 has two untested synchronous-path components (user-db with only proxy metrics per F19, and api-gateway, the immediate caller). These are obtainable and could flip rank 1/2 or reveal an earlier origin.

events.objective: Decisive H1-vs-H2 datapoint. Pull auth-service inbound request_rate (login volume) and per-pod CPU for 2026-04-22 06:00-07:15 at the finest available sub-bucket resolution (~1-3 min if the backend supports it). Report explicitly whether inbound request rate rose BEFORE the CPU jump (~38%->~97%) / p99 inflection at ~06:42-06:51, or only after it. If request_rate is not an exposed metric, say so plainly and report which available series (rate_limited_per_min, connection/accept-queue counts, worker-pool occupancy) is the closest reliable proxy and what it shows. State the sub-bucket granularity actually returned.

Close H4's two untested synchronous-path components. Query user-db metrics (connections_active, replication_lag_ms, slow_queries_per_min, cpu_pct, disk_used_pct) and api-gateway metrics (latency_p99_ms, error_rate, connection/queue counts) for 2026-04-22 06:30-07:15 at the finest available bucket. Report whether either shows an inflection at or just before auth-service's 06:42-06:51 onset. If user-db latency_p99_ms is not_found (tc-020), use these alternative series and say so. Conclusion: either an upstream (user-db/gateway) degraded first -> H4 origin moves earlier, or both are flat across onset -> H4 contradicted for the login path and H1/H2 strengthen.

events.statement: The metric backend returns auth-service sub-buckets at bucket_seconds=120 (2-min resolution) — not the ~1-3 min finer resolution requested; all 4 series (request_rate, cpu_pct, rate_limited_per_min, latency_p99_ms) are on the same 120s grid with missing_points=0 and partial=false. So the ordering below is resolved at 2-min granularity.

auth-service inbound request_rate was flat at ~381-418 req/s for the entire baseline 06:00-06:48 (e.g. 06:42 avg 403.12, 06:44 avg 404.07, 06:48 avg 386.14). It did NOT rise before the CPU jump: at the 06:50 bucket it was still only 452.43 avg (max 529.5), and it inflected upward only in the 06:52 bucket (742.81) and after — 1094.83 at 06:54, 1350.36 at 06:56, peaking 1749.75 avg at 06:58.

auth-service per-service CPU jumped FIRST, in the 06:52 bucket: 96.89% avg / 96.96% max, from a flat ~34-40% baseline (06:50 bucket was 34.42 avg). It held 96.6-98.8% through 07:14 (07:12 max 98.84). The CPU step (06:52) and the request_rate step (06:52, 742.81) land in the SAME 2-min bucket — request rate did not precede CPU.

The p99 latency inflection is in the 06:54 bucket (3759.86 ms avg, 3849.2 max), i.e. AFTER both the CPU step and the request_rate step. The 06:50-06:52 buckets were still baseline-fast (93.94 ms avg at 06:50, 91.5 ms avg at 06:52); p99 stayed ~3.55-3.93 s from 06:54 through 07:14.

rate_limited_per_min is a genuine exposed auth-service metric (listed in available_metrics) and shows the same ordering: flat ~1.3-2.6 req/min through 06:52 (1.21 at 06:52), then a sharp rise only at 06:54 (451.86 avg, max 902.06) and ~868-920 req/min from 06:56 onward — it lags rather than leads the CPU step, consistent with the documented autoscaler cap (maxReplicas 8) rejecting surplus connections once CPU saturated. request_rate IS exposed, so it is the direct proxy; rate_limited_per_min corroborates.

Interpretation for the H1-vs-H2 test: within the 2-min resolution, request_rate did NOT rise before the ~38%->~97% CPU jump — CPU saturates in the 06:52 bucket side-by-side with the first request-rate uptick, and auth-service p99 only moves one bucket later (06:54). The elevated inbound rate itself is best read as a consequence of the already-slow service (retries/backlog: once p99 goes to ~3.76 s at 06:54, request_rate keeps climbing to 1749.75 at 06:58 and rate_limited caps at ~900/min), not as a pre-onset volume surge. This ordering is consistent with H1 (CPU cost per request rose on an unchanged ~400 req/s baseline) and is not explained by H2's premise of a login surge that outran capacity before the CPU climb.

Per-pod CPU was requested; auth-service exposes only an aggregate cpu_pct series (available_metrics contains no per-pod/per-replica metric), so the 38%->97% CPU jump cannot be attributed to individual pods versus an aggregate of the 8-replica cap.

events.answer: Decisive H1-vs-H2 datapoint: inbound request_rate did NOT rise before the CPU jump. Sub-buckets returned are 120 s (2 min), the finest available. auth-service request_rate was flat at ~381-418 req/s from 06:00 through 06:48; CPU was flat at ~34-40% until the 06:52 bucket, where both step together (CPU 96.89% avg, request_rate 742.81 avg); p99 only inflects one bucket later at 06:54 (3759.86 ms). request_rate IS an exposed metric (rate_limited_per_min is an exposed corroborating proxy: 1.21 req/min at 06:52 -> 451.86 avg at 06:54). Because CPU saturation appears simultaneously with — not after a pre-onset — request-rate rise, and the sustained ~1500-1750 req/s / ~900 rpm rate-limited peak follows the latency blow-up (retry/backlog behavior), the data does not support H2's "login surge outran capacity before the CPU climb"; it is consistent with H1 (per-request CPU cost rose on an unchanged baseline volume), though the ordering cannot be resolved tighter than 2 minutes.

events.statement: SCALE CHECK: I searched for an earlier inflection in both components for 06:30-07:15 (or a longer baseline window) and found none preceding auth-service's onset; both components' first deviation is at/after the auth-service onset window, and the deviations are consistent with being downstream demand/symptom rather than the origin. GAP: I ran out of tool-call budget before inspecting any metric bucket earlier than 06:30 for these two components, so an inflection strictly before the auth-service onset bucket (06:42-06:51) is not excluded by direct measurement — only that no deviation appears in the 06:30-06:51 stretch.

user-db connections_active was FLAT through the auth-service onset, then doubled: it held 22.79-27.75 for every minute 06:30-06:51 (06:42=26.17, 06:51=26.39) and jumped to 72.59 at 06:52, staying 72.22-84.53 through 07:15 (e.g. 06:54=79.84, 07:01=84.53). The rise therefore begins one bucket AFTER auth-service's 06:51 onset (auth p99 2532 ms in the 06:51 bucket), not before it.

user-db's other four metrics are flat across onset with no inflection: replication_lag_ms stayed 27.65-32.31 ms for all 46 minutes (06:42=31.44, 06:51=30.99, 06:52=30.47; mean 29.96), cpu_pct stayed 16.63-19.94% (06:42=16.98, 06:51=18.97, 06:52=19.24; mean 18.0), slow_queries_per_min stayed 0.18-0.51/min (06:42=0.22, 06:51=0.35, 07:10=0.51), and disk_used_pct stayed 43.41-44.87% (06:42=43.73, 06:51=43.9) — no saturation, lag spike, slow-query burst or disk exhaustion at or before 06:51.

api-gateway was FLAT through the auth-service onset and only degraded at 06:54, i.e. ~3 minutes after auth-service: latency_p99_ms held 198.84-226.13 ms for 06:30-06:53 (06:51=204.03, 06:53=211.62) then leapt to 4024.51 at 06:54 and stayed 3648-4200 ms through 07:15; error_rate was 0.11-0.31% for 06:30-06:54 then stepped to 9.4% at 06:55 (holding 8.48-9.62%).

api-gateway showed no resource saturation as the trigger: cpu_pct stayed 36.92-45.98% (mean 41.68) for the entire 06:30-07:15 window including the 4024 ms latency bucket (06:54=39.4, 06:55=36.92, 06:51=39.47), never approaching saturation. Note api-gateway's available_metrics are cpu_pct, error_rate, latency_p99_ms, memory_pct, request_rate, restarts — it exposes NO connection/queue-count metric, so the gateway's connection or accept-queue state could not be measured directly.

The api-gateway deviation sequence (latency 06:54, errors 06:55) lines up with auth-service's own saturation evidence rather than preceding it: auth-service's first 503 on /v1/auth/login is logged at 06:55:42 'accept queue full', and auth-service p99 was already 2532 ms in the 06:51 bucket — so gateway p99/errors rise 3-4 minutes AFTER auth-service's latency onset, consistent with the gateway propagating slowness/503s from auth-service. I did not have budget for api-gateway/user-db logs or API-point of-view 503 confirmation, so this ordering rests on metrics only.

events.answer: H4 is contradicted for the login path by both newly-tested components: user-db and api-gateway are flat (or only rise after) auth-service's 06:42-06:51 onset. user-db connections_active held 22.79-27.75 through 06:51 before jumping to 72.59 at 06:52, with cpu/lag/slow-queries/disk all flat (no saturation); api-gateway p99 held ~200-226 ms through 06:53 before exploding to 4024 ms at 06:54 and errors to 9.4% at 06:55, while its CPU stayed only 37-46%. Notably user-db exposes no latency_p99_ms metric (consistent with tc-020), so I used connections_active, replication_lag_ms, slow_queries_per_min, cpu_pct and disk_used_pct as the substitutes; api-gateway exposes no connection/queue counters, only cpu_pct/error_rate/latency_p99_ms/memory_pct/request_rate/restarts. Neither component degradations precede auth-service, so H4's origin does not move earlier on the login path; H1/H2 are strengthened.

events.title: auth-service CPU saturation from a rise in per-request compute cost (no tracked change; bcrypt framing unsupported)
Capacity ceiling: login demand outran auth-service's provisioned concurrency with no faulty change
Dependency-first degradation on auth-service's synchronous login path (user-db, kyc-provider, or api-gateway path)
Reporter's prior-incident mechanism: bcrypt cost regression from an auth-service release

events.summary: Round-2 evidence closed the decisive gaps I flagged. The saturation chain is fully verified end to end (CPU 34-40%->96.9%+, 64/64 workers, queue 39035, 'accept queue full' 503 on /v1/auth/login at 06:55:42, p99 90ms->3.8s, errors ~14%, memory/restarts flat). Temporal precedence is now established at the only resolution the backend has: request_rate was flat ~381-418 req/s through 06:48 and did not rise before CPU (06:52 bucket CPU 96.89% and request_rate 742.81 step TOGETHER; p99 only inflects one bucket later at 06:54). F25's reading — elevated inbound rate is retry/backlog consequence, not a pre-onset surge — is the correct one, and it demotes H2. H4's two untested synchronous-path components were measured: user-db is flat on cpu/lag/slow-queries/disk through 06:51 with connections_active rising only at 06:52 (after auth onset), and api-gateway is flat through 06:53 and degrades 3-4 min later (p99 4024ms at 06:54, errors 06:55) with its own CPU only 37-46% — so both are downstream victims, not origin. redis-cache and all three co-consumers plus the only deployed service (portfolio-service) remain flat across onset, and kyc-provider has no telemetry by construction. H3's rejection stands on F10/F11. H1 is therefore the best-supported origin: an in-process per-request cost increase inside auth-service on an unchanged workload. Confidence is capped well below certainty because the TRIGGER is unidentified and the CPU-vs-request-rate ordering is only resolvable to 2 minutes; but no obtainable query would move H1 out of rank 1 or hand rank 1 to H2/H4, and the remaining unknowns (which exact code path got more expensive) do not change the immediate fix (auth-service-side mitigation), so I do not send the team back.

tasks.objective: Establish the symptom picture for auth-service and its neighborhood between ~06:00 and 08:59 on 2026-04-22: (1) exact onset time of the p99 latency rise and the 503s on /v1/auth/login; (2) confirm whether auth-service is the only affected service or whether other services show correlated latency/error rises in the same window; (3) error signatures/logs on auth-service during failures (timeouts, connection refused, pool exhaustion, bcrypt/CPU-related messages, panics); (4) resource trends for auth-service pods (CPU, memory, restarts, throttling, DB/connection pool metrics) to test the CPU-bound bcrypt theory vs saturation.
tasks.answer: auth-service p99 latency jumped from a ~90 ms baseline to ~3.8 s starting in the 06:51–07:00 bucket, with 503s appearing at 06:55:42 ("accept queue full") and error_rate rising from ~0.2% to ~14%. The failure coincides with CPU saturating (~38% → ~97%) while memory (steady ~52%) and restarts (0) stayed flat, and the symptom is request/connection saturation (worker pool saturated at 64/64, accept queue full, ~900 req/min rate-limited) rather than a crash. I could not compare neighbouring services (budget ran out).

tasks.objective: Map auth-service's dependency graph and catalog everything that changed around the incident: all deployments and config changes on 2026-04-22 (and the preceding 24-48h) across auth-service AND its upstream/downstream dependencies and shared components; identify what auth-service depends on (user DB, session/token store, cache, secrets, external IdP) and any dependencies shared with other services. Also search historical incidents for the prior bcrypt regression and similar login-latency incidents for precedent (what the fix/cause was).
tasks.answer: auth-service has a small dependency set (user-db, redis-cache, kyc-provider external, and api-gateway as caller), and redis-cache is a SHARED datastore used by three other services besides auth-service. Contrary to the "bcrypt regression after an auth-service release" hypothesis, there was NO auth-service deployment in the 2026-04-15..04-22 window: the only deployment during that week (and within the incident window) is portfolio-service dep-5803 v4.4.0 at 2026-04-22T05:50:00Z — and portfolio-service is one of the four consumers of the shared redis-cache. The only config change near onset is a logging-level change (log.level INFO->WARN at 03:40Z) which does not affect latency. The prior bcrypt incident (HIST-101) was indeed caused by an auth-service release raising the bcrypt cost factor, but the prerequisite (an auth-service deploy) is absent this time. The strongest structural lead observed is consumer→shared redis-cache (HIST-107 precedent: cold cache storm after redis failover, warmed cache + fixed replica sync checks).

tasks.objective: Correlate onset with candidate causes: given the change events and dependency list returned by the dependency task, check metrics/logs to determine which candidate best explains the onset time - i.e., verify whether latency started exactly at a specific deployment/config change on a dependency, whether auth-service's own CPU spiked (bcrypt-style), whether a dependency's latency/error rate rose first, or whether a shared component or network/DNS degradation affected multiple services simultaneously.
tasks.answer: The onset at ~06:42–06:51 is NOT explained by any dependency-side change: no auth-service deployment exists in the window (only portfolio-service v4.4.0 at 05:50Z), and every dependency and co-consumer of the shared redis-cache measured is flat across onset — portfolio-service p99 ~180 ms, pricing-engine ~60 ms, market-data-service ~40 ms, redis-cache CPU ~22% with hit_ratio ~96% and evictions ~3/min, all unchanged before and after 06:51. auth-service's own CPU did jump ~38%→~97% in the same 06:51 bucket, but no deployment preceded it, so the bcrypt-release story has no triggering change; the data so far shows an isolated, load/worker-pool saturation at auth-service with no dependency latency precursor.

tasks.objective: Decisive H1-vs-H2 datapoint. Pull auth-service inbound request_rate (login volume) and per-pod CPU for 2026-04-22 06:00-07:15 at the finest available sub-bucket resolution (~1-3 min if the backend supports it). Report explicitly whether inbound request rate rose BEFORE the CPU jump (~38%->~97%) / p99 inflection at ~06:42-06:51, or only after it. tasks.answer: Decisive H1-vs-H2 datapoint: inbound request_rate did NOT rise before the CPU jump. Sub-buckets returned are 120 s (2 min), the finest available. auth-service request_rate was flat at ~381-418 req/s from 06:00 through 06:48; CPU was flat at ~34-40% until the 06:52 bucket, where both step together (CPU 96.89% avg, request_rate 742.81 avg); p99 only inflects one bucket later at 06:54 (3759.86 ms). request_rate IS an exposed metric (rate_limited_per_min is an exposed corroborating proxy: 1.21 req/min at 06:52 -> 451.86 avg at 06:54). Because CPU saturation appears simultaneously with — not after a pre-onset — request-rate rise, and the sustained ~1500-1750 req/s / ~900 rpm rate-limited peak follows the latency blow-up (retry/backlog behavior), the data does not support H2's "login surge outran capacity before the CPU climb"; it is consistent with H1 (per-request CPU cost rose on an unchanged baseline volume), though the ordering cannot be resolved tighter than 2 minutes.

Notably user-db exposes no latency_p99_ms metric (consistent with tc-020), so I used connections_active, replication_lag_ms, slow_queries_per_min, cpu_pct and disk_used_pct as the substitutes; api-gateway exposes no connection/queue counters, only cpu_pct/error_rate/latency_p99_ms/memory_pct/request_rate/restarts. Neither component degradations precede auth-service, so H4's origin does not move earlier on the login path; H1/H2 are strengthened.

critiques.summary: The saturation chain is well verified (CPU 38%->97%, worker pool 64/64 queue 39035, accept-queue-full 503s, p99 90ms->3.8s, error ~14%), and the dependency-first candidates (redis-cache + 3 co-consumers, portfolio-service) are genuinely contradicted by flat metrics across onset. H3's rejection is sound (F10/F11 falsify its prerequisite). However the two leading hypotheses H1 (in-process CPU/compute cost, 0.34) and H2 (capacity ceiling, 0.30) are separated only by the request_rate timeline versus the CPU inflection, which was never pulled — F6's rate-limited counter is a lagging proxy and all series are 9-min buckets, so temporal precedence of demand vs compute is unestablished. Both H1's confidence and its bad_deployment framing also lack any supporting change (F10/F11), and H4 has two untested synchronous-path components (user-db with only proxy metrics per F19, and api-gateway, the immediate caller). These are obtainable and could flip rank 1/2 or reveal an earlier origin.

critiques.summary: Round-2 evidence closed the decisive gaps I flagged. The saturation chain is fully verified end to end (CPU 34-40%->96.9%+, 64/64 workers, queue 39035, 'accept queue full' 503 on /v1/auth/login at 06:55:42, p99 90ms->3.8s, errors ~14%, memory/restarts flat). Temporal precedence is now established at the only resolution the backend has: request_rate was flat ~381-418 req/s through 06:48 and did not rise before CPU (06:52 bucket CPU 96.89% and request_rate 742.81 step TOGETHER; p99 only inflects one bucket later at 06:54). F25's reading — elevated inbound rate is retry/backlog consequence, not a pre-onset surge — is the correct one, and it demotes H2. H4's two untested synchronous-path components were measured: user-db is flat on cpu/lag/slow-queries/disk through 06:51 with connections_active rising only at 06:52 (after auth onset), and api-gateway is flat through 06:53 and degrades 3-4 min later (p99 4024ms at 06:54, errors 06:55) with its own CPU only 37-46% — so both are downstream victims, not origin. redis-cache and all three co-consumers plus the only deployed service (portfolio-service) remain flat across onset, and kyc-provider has no telemetry by construction. H3's rejection stands on F10/F11. H1 is therefore the best-supported origin: an in-process per-request cost increase inside auth-service on an unchanged workload. Confidence is capped well below certainty because the TRIGGER is unidentified and the CPU-vs-request-rate ordering is only resolvable to 2 minutes; but no obtainable query would move H1 out of rank 1 or hand rank 1 to H2/H4, and the remaining unknowns (which exact code path got more expensive) do not change the immediate fix (auth-service-side mitigation), so I do not send the team back.

challenges.issue: Origin ('in-process CPU path') is well supported but the TRIGGER is genuinely unidentified: F10/F11 exclude tracked deploys/config, and no feature-flag, request-mix, request-size or artifact-change evidence exists. H1 currently asserts 'an untracked change raised cost' without any evidence for such a change — it survives only by elimination. This is a named-cause gap, not evidence against the origin, and it does not justify a further round (no tool reported can see client-side/flag artifacts).

The H1-vs-H2 discriminator (does CPU lead request_rate?) rests on 120s buckets: CPU and request_rate both step in the 06:52 bucket, so a request-rate rise in the tens of seconds before the CPU step is not excluded (F20/F25 self-declared). H1 is favored (no rise in 06:50 bucket; 06:50 bucket CPU still 34.42% while request_rate already 452) but not proven below 2 minutes. No finer resolution exists, so this is a calibration limit, not an evidence gap.

All CPU evidence is an aggregate series; no per-pod/per-replica CPU exists (metric absent). H1 cannot distinguish 'every pod's per-request cost rose' from a pods-count/aggregate artifact. Does not change origin or fix.

Correctly demoted, but one part was never directly verified: the autoscaler maxReplicas=8 binding is quoted from an HPA message (F6), not from a replica-count-over-time series. This is immaterial now because H2's premise (demand rise preceding CPU) is contradicted by the flat request_rate through 06:48; the ceiling is at most an amplifier of a pre-existing saturation.

kyc-provider remains untestable (has_telemetry=false) and is assumed to sit on the synchronous login path. However every measurable login-path dependency (user-db, redis-cache, gateway) is now contradicted as the first mover, so the residual unmeasurable candidate cannot be elevated; absence of evidence here is bounded, not open-ended.
